unit.title: Apply the principles of contract law

summary: This unit teaches managers the principles of contract law. You will learn what makes an agreement a valid contract, how offer and acceptance work, how terms and defects are treated, what remedies follow a breach, how contracts end, and how to review, manage and settle disputes over contracts in a Jamaican business or public body.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors, managers and owners who sign, approve or manage contracts for Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies: supply of goods, services, building work, hire, employment-related services and sales. A **contract** is an agreement that the law will enforce. Contract law tells you when you are bound, what you are bound to do, what happens if someone breaks the agreement and how disputes are settled.

Jamaican contract law rests mainly on common-law principles, with statutes added for particular matters such as the sale of goods, consumer protection, electronic transactions and arbitration. This kit refers to those laws by their purpose only. You are not being trained to be a lawyer. You are being trained to spot the legal issues, avoid common mistakes, keep good records and know when to take legal advice.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your unit
rows: Decide whether a valid contract exists
Test an agreement for offer, acceptance, consideration, intention, capacity, certainty and legality.
Trace offer and acceptance
Follow quotations, replies, counter-offers, withdrawals and acceptances, and say when a contract was formed.
Read and classify terms
Tell express from implied terms, conditions from warranties, and judge exclusion clauses.
Spot defects in agreement
Recognise misrepresentation, mistake, duress and illegality and their effects.
Handle breach and remedies
Identify a breach and work out damages; know when specific performance, an injunction or rescission is used.
End and change contracts

Manage contracts and disputes
Check before signing, monitor performance, keep records and choose negotiation, mediation, arbitration or court.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with short business scenarios and some sums.

A written paper with short answers (exact terms such as consideration, counter-offer, liquidated damages) and longer answers where you analyse a sequence of emails, calculate damages or advise on a dispute.
Group practical tasks: reviewing a draft supply contract, and tracing a contract's formation, calculating a claim and role-playing a settlement.

blocks.note: Contract problems are solved by applying a rule to the facts. In every scenario, write the rule first, then apply it to the facts, then state the result.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: What a contract is and when the law enforces it

blocks.p: A contract is a legally binding agreement. Not every agreement is a contract: a promise to meet a friend for lunch is not. For a contract to be **valid and enforceable**, these elements must be present.

head: Element
Question to ask
Example of a failure
rows: Offer
Did one party clearly state terms on which it is willing to be bound?
A shop price list is only an invitation to treat
Acceptance
Did the other party agree to exactly those terms, and tell the offeror?
A reply that changes the price is a counter-offer
Consideration
Did each side give or promise something of value?
A promise to pay for work already completed
Intention to create legal relations
Did the parties mean to be legally bound?
A family or social arrangement
Capacity
Is each party legally able to contract?
A very young person; a company officer with no authority
Certainty
Are the terms clear enough to enforce?
"Price to be agreed later" with no way to fix it
Legality
Is the purpose lawful?
An agreement to pay a bribe

ul: **Spoken (oral) contracts** are binding, but hard to prove when a dispute arises.
**Written contracts** give clear evidence of the agreed terms. Put important contracts in writing even when the law does not require it.
**Contracts by electronic means** (emails, online forms, clicking "I agree") can form contracts if the terms were available and the person agreed, under the electronic transactions law.
**Deeds** are formal documents, signed and witnessed as the law requires, and need no consideration.
**Contracts the law says must be in writing**, or evidenced in writing, include contracts for the sale of land. Check with an attorney.

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: Void
The law treats it as never having been a contract
An agreement for an illegal purpose
Voidable
Valid until the innocent party chooses to set it aside
A contract made because of a false statement or duress
Unenforceable
A court will not order it to be carried out
A contract that should have been in writing and was not

blocks.note: Always ask first: **who exactly is bound, to do what, and by when?** Many disputes come from not naming the parties correctly, or from leaving the work and the price unclear.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **offer** is a statement of willingness to be bound on certain terms, which becomes a contract once it is accepted. An **invitation to treat** invites others to make offers. Examples of invitations to treat: goods displayed with a price, a catalogue or price list, an advertisement, a call for quotations. A **quotation** sent in reply to a request, with clear quantity, price and delivery, is usually an offer. A tender call is an invitation; each bid is an offer.

ul: Acceptance must be **unconditional**: agreement to all the terms as offered.
It must be **communicated** to the person who made the offer. Silence is not acceptance, and an offeror cannot say that silence will count as acceptance.
It may be by words, in writing, by electronic message or by conduct (for example, starting work as the offer invited).
It must follow the **method** the offer asks for, if it states one.

For acceptance by post, the general rule is that it is complete when the letter is properly posted, if post is a reasonable way to reply. For instant methods such as phone calls and, usually, emails, it is complete when the message is received.

blocks.p: A reply that adds or changes terms is a **counter-offer**. It **rejects** the original offer and ends it. The original offer cannot later be accepted unless it is made again. A request for information ("Is delivery included?") is not a counter-offer and does not end the offer.

head: Way the offer ends
Meaning
rows: Rejection or counter-offer
The other party says no or changes the terms
Withdrawal (revocation)
The offeror takes the offer back **before it is accepted**, and the offeree is told. A promise to keep an offer open is not binding unless the offeree paid for it.
Lapse
The time stated in the offer runs out, or a reasonable time passes
Death or loss of capacity
Depends on the type of contract

head: Date and message
Legal effect
rows: Monday: a supplier's quotation, "40 chairs at J$7,000 each, delivered by 20 March, open until Friday"
Offer
Tuesday: the buyer's reply, "We will pay J$6,500"
Counter-offer; the original offer ends
Wednesday: the supplier replies, "Our price is J$7,000"
A new offer by the supplier
Thursday: the buyer's reply, "Agreed at J$7,000"
Acceptance of the new offer; **contract formed on Thursday**

blocks.p: In the timeline, the contract exists on Thursday because the supplier made a fresh offer on Wednesday. If the supplier had only said "Sorry, we cannot lower the price" (refusing without repeating the offer), then the Thursday message would be a new offer from the buyer, which the supplier would still have to accept.

blocks.note: A manager who wants to keep an offer open should say so clearly ("valid until 5 p.m. on Friday 12 June"). A manager who wants to avoid being bound by a message should mark it "subject to contract" or say it is an invitation, and should reply to every offer promptly in writing.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: The other requirements: consideration, intention, capacity, certainty and legality

blocks.p: **Consideration** is the price paid for a promise: something of value that each party gives or promises, such as money, goods, services or an agreement to give something up. It must be real, but it need not match the value. Selling an old printer to a staff member for J$1,000 is valid even if it is worth more, because courts do not weigh the bargain.

ul: **Past consideration is not good:** a promise to pay for work already done, made afterwards, is generally not enforceable unless the work was requested and payment was expected.
**Performing an existing legal duty** is generally not new consideration.
A **deposit or part payment** is usually part of consideration and shows the agreement is serious.

blocks.p: In **commercial** agreements, the law presumes the parties intend to be legally bound. In **social and family** arrangements, the law presumes they do not. Either presumption can be rebutted by clear evidence. A sponsorship letter between a company and an event organiser, which says "this agreement is binding", shows intention. A phrase such as "honourable pledge only" may show the opposite, so use it carefully.

ul: **Minors** (people under the age of majority) have limited capacity. Contracts for necessaries, such as food, clothing and basic needs, can be enforced; most other contracts are not binding on a minor. Do not sell large items on credit to a minor.

**Companies** act only through people. Before signing, confirm that the person has **authority** to bind the company: ask for a director's resolution, a letter of authority or the company's signing policy. A firm that holds someone out as having authority may be bound even if the person was not authorised, but do not depend on that.
Persons of unsound mind or under the influence of drink or drugs may lack capacity if the other side knew.
**Public bodies** may contract only within their powers and must follow the procurement rules that apply to them.

blocks.p: The terms must be clear enough to enforce: the parties, the goods or services, the quantity, the price (or a method of working it out) and the time. An "agreement to agree" later on an essential term, with no way to fix it, may be too uncertain to bind.

ul: Contracts to commit a crime, to pay or take a bribe, to defraud the tax authority or to supply goods that the law forbids are **illegal and void or unenforceable**.

Contracts against public policy, such as unreasonable restraints on trade, may not be enforced. A restriction on a former employee working in the same trade must protect a real business interest and go no further than needed.

blocks.note: A manager must never sign, or ask a supplier to sign, an arrangement that hides payments from the tax authority, pays a public officer to speed up an approval or avoids the procurement rules. Such agreements are unlawful and may bring criminal and disciplinary action.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Express terms** are those the parties actually state and agree, in writing or by word of mouth. **Implied terms** are not stated but are brought in by law or by custom or necessity. The sale of goods law implies terms into sales by a business: the seller has the right to sell, the goods match their description, and they are of satisfactory quality and fit for the purpose made known. **Consumer protection law** gives members of the public rights that a seller's own terms cannot remove.

head: Type
Meaning
If it is broken
Example
rows: Condition
A major term that goes to the root of the contract
The innocent party may end the contract and claim damages
A hotel double-books the date of a wedding reception
Warranty
A minor term
Damages only; the contract continues
Chairs delivered in a slightly different shade of grey
Intermediate (innominate) term
Importance depends on how serious the breach is
Depends on the effect of the breach
Late delivery by one day, of a non-urgent order

blocks.p: Whether a term is a condition or a warranty depends on its importance, and on what the contract says. Time is often treated as a condition in commercial contracts when the contract says "time is of the essence" or the date is critical.

An **exclusion clause** excludes or limits one party's liability. It is effective only if it was **made known and became part of the contract before it was agreed**, for example in the signed document. A clause on an invoice or receipt handed over after the deal was made is usually too late. Courts read exclusion clauses strictly, and the law forbids excluding some liabilities altogether, such as for death or injury caused by negligence, and limits the use of such clauses against consumers.

Suppliers often print standard terms on the back of quotations, orders and invoices. **Read them.** If you sign or accept the quotation, the terms may become part of the contract. Where each side tries to use its own standard terms, ask for a single negotiated document.

blocks.note: Before signing, ask: what does this clause let the other side do, and what does it stop me doing? Mark any one-sided clause (limits on liability, automatic renewals, high late fees, termination on short notice) for negotiation or legal advice.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: When agreement goes wrong: misrepresentation, mistake and duress

blocks.p: A contract may be binding in form but affected by a defect in how it was made.

head: Defect
What it is
Business example
Usual effect
rows: Misrepresentation
A false statement of fact that induces a party to contract
A seller says a van has done 40,000 km when it has done 140,000 km
The contract may be set aside (rescission); damages may be available, especially for fraud or carelessness
Mistake
A serious error shared or known to the other side about a basic fact
Both parties believe goods exist that were already destroyed
May make the contract void; the courts are strict about this
Duress
Illegitimate pressure, such as threats to a person or property
A supplier threatens to damage property unless the contract is signed
The contract may be set aside
Undue influence
Improper use of a position of trust or power
A trusted adviser pressures a vulnerable client
The contract may be set aside
Illegality
An unlawful purpose or performance
An agreement to pay a bribe
Void or unenforceable

blocks.p: A statement made before the contract is a **term** if the parties meant it to be part of the agreement, for example a written specification. It is a **representation** if it only induced the agreement. Both can give remedies: a broken term gives a claim for breach, and a false representation can give rescission or damages. Keep a record of what was said and written during negotiations.

blocks.h: Practical steps for a business buyer who relied on a false statement

flow: Gather evidence of the statement (emails, quotations, notes)
Notify the seller in writing promptly
Stop using the goods or services if possible; delay can be treated as accepting them
Take legal advice on setting the contract aside and claiming damages

blocks.note: Rescission is usually lost if you delay, keep using the goods as if all were well, or if third parties have acquired rights. Act quickly.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **breach** happens when a party does not perform, performs late, performs badly or says in advance that it will not perform. An **anticipatory breach** is a clear statement, before the date, that a party will not perform. The innocent party may treat the contract as ended, or wait for performance, but must be careful: delay can increase loss.

**Damages** are money paid to compensate the innocent party. The aim is to put that party **in the position it would have been in if the contract had been performed**, not to punish the other side. Three principles control the amount.

head: Principle
Meaning
rows: Causation
The loss must be caused by the breach
Remoteness

Only losses that were foreseeable when the contract was made are recovered: losses that arise naturally from the breach, or that the other party knew about. Special loss the other side never knew about is usually not recoverable.
Mitigation
The innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce its loss (for example buy replacements promptly, or look for a new tenant). It cannot claim for loss it could have avoided.

blocks.p: A restaurant orders 8 freezers at J$85,000 each. The supplier fails to deliver. The restaurant buys 8 equivalent freezers elsewhere at J$93,000 each and pays J$6,000 for extra transport. It also claims J$250,000 lost profit on a catering job that the supplier knew nothing about.

head: Item
Working
Recoverable?
rows: Extra cost of replacements
Yes
Extra transport
Yes, as it arose naturally
Lost profit on the unknown job
No, too remote
**Likely damages**
Total

blocks.p: **Liquidated damages** are a sum fixed in the contract in advance as a genuine estimate of loss if a party breaks a term, such as a completion date. Example: J$30,000 for each day of late completion. If the work is 7 days late, the owner can claim 7 × J$30,000 = J$210,000, without proving actual loss. A sum that is **far more than any genuine loss**, meant to frighten the party into performing, is a **penalty** and the court may refuse to enforce it.

head: Remedy
What it does
When it is used
rows: Specific performance
A court order to carry out the contract
Where money is not enough, such as a contract to buy a particular piece of land or a unique item. The court decides; it is not automatic.
Injunction
A court order to stop doing something
To enforce a promise not to do something, such as using a brand after a licence has ended
Rescission
Undoing the contract and returning the parties to their position before it
Misrepresentation, duress and similar defects
Termination
Ending the contract for a serious breach (breach of condition, or repudiation)
Where the breach goes to the root of the contract

blocks.p: Before going to court, the innocent party normally sends a **letter of claim**: it sets out the contract, the breach, the loss with the figures, what is demanded and a date for reply. Keep it factual and polite and keep copies. Settlement discussions often follow.

blocks.note: When you calculate damages, list each loss, say how it was worked out, and then say whether it is recoverable and why. Work every sum twice.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Ending contracts, managing performance and settling disputes

head: Way
Meaning
Example
rows: Performance
Both sides do what they promised exactly
Goods delivered and paid for
Agreement
Both sides agree to end it or replace it, usually giving each other something
Two firms end a service contract early and agree the final payment
Breach
One side breaks a condition or refuses to perform; the other chooses to end it
A hotel cannot host the event on the date promised
Frustration
An unforeseen event, not the fault of either party, makes performance impossible or radically different
A building is destroyed by fire before the event; the parties are released and the contract ends automatically

blocks.p: Frustration is narrow: a contract that has simply become harder or more costly is not frustrated. Contracts often contain a **force majeure** clause that says what happens when events outside the parties' control, such as a hurricane or flood, prevent performance. Read it.

A change in what has been agreed needs the **agreement of both sides**. One party cannot change the terms alone. For any change in scope, price or dates, agree a **written variation** signed by both, referring to the original contract. A spoken or informal promise on a site visit is hard to prove and may not bind the firm.

ol: Define the need clearly: what, how much, by when, to what standard.
Follow the organisation's purchasing procedure; get competing quotations; for a public body, follow the procurement rules.
Check the other party: its legal name, licence, insurance, references and the authority of the person who will sign.
Read **every** term. Check scope, price, payment terms, delivery, quality standards, penalties, termination rights, liability limits and how disputes are settled.
Get legal advice where unsure, and before agreeing anything that is large, long or unusual.
Confirm that the contract is signed by authorised people and that each party gets a signed copy.

ul: Summarise key obligations, dates, payment stages and notice requirements, and share them with everyone involved.
Name one person responsible for the contract.
Meet regularly; keep minutes and records; confirm any spoken instruction in writing the same day.
Check work against the specification before approving payment.
Raise problems early and in writing; do not wait until the final date.
Diarise review, renewal and notice dates.
Handle every change as a written variation.

head: Method
What happens
Strengths
Limits
rows: Negotiation
The parties talk directly
Cheap, private, quick, protects the relationship
May fail if positions are fixed
Mediation
A neutral mediator helps the parties reach their own agreement
Private, flexible, low cost, often works
The mediator cannot impose a result
Arbitration
A neutral arbitrator hears both sides and gives a decision that binds them, if the parties agreed to it
Private, expert, usually faster than court
Costs can be high; limited appeal
Court action
A judge decides
Binding and enforceable; can order remedies
Public, slow and costly; relationships suffer

blocks.p: Many contracts set out a ladder: negotiate first, then mediate, then arbitrate or go to court. In Jamaica, mediation services are available through the courts and through bodies such as the Dispute Resolution Foundation. Choose the method that fits the amount, the need for privacy and whether the relationship must continue.

blocks.note: Keep a contract file for every important contract: signed copy, drafts, emails, minutes, variations, delivery notes, inspection reports and payment records. In a dispute, the side with the better records usually has the stronger case.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: list the elements of a valid contract and test an agreement against them.
explain the difference between an offer and an invitation to treat, and between acceptance and a counter-offer.
say when acceptance is complete and how an offer can end.
explain consideration, including why past consideration fails and why value need not be equal.

identify a breach, including anticipatory breach.

c1.title: Desks for a school in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: The board of a high school in Savanna-la-Mar asked Hanover Office Furniture for a quotation for 60 student desks. On 1 June the supplier emailed: 60 desks at J$9,500 each, delivery within 21 days of order, "offer open until 12 June". On 8 June, the supplier's sales manager phoned the school bursar to say that the offer was withdrawn because the desks had been promised to another school. On 10 June the board secretary emailed, "We accept your quotation of 1 June." The board wants the desks at the quoted price.

c2.title: A second-hand oven in May Pen
c2.text: Mrs Gloria Ricketts, who owns a bakery in May Pen, bought a second-hand deck oven for J$650,000. The dealer had told her, "It was serviced every year and is in perfect order." After delivery, the dealer handed her an invoice that said "sold as seen; no liability for faults". The oven's heating element failed in the second week, and an engineer told her the oven had never been serviced and had a cracked element when sold. Mrs Ricketts wants to return the oven and recover her money.

c3.title: Road gravel for a municipal corporation
c3.text: The Morant Bay municipal corporation plans a 12-month contract for road-repair gravel. A supplier's sales representative, Mr Ricardo Hines, says he will sign "for the company", but the supplier's board says that only directors may sign contracts of this size. The draft allows the supplier to stop deliveries at any time without liability. The procurement officer, Mrs Pauline Walters, is told by a friend of the supplier that "a little something" for her would speed up the approval.

c4.title: A display fridge for an Ocho Rios restaurant
c4.text: An Ocho Rios restaurant ordered a refrigerated display unit from a Kingston dealer for J$420,000, delivery by 1 December. The contract included a clause: "J$12,000 for each day of delay". The dealer did not deliver. On 6 December the restaurant bought an equivalent unit elsewhere for J$468,000 and paid J$9,000 extra for delivery. The restaurant also says it lost a J$300,000 catering job for Christmas, which it never told the dealer about.

c5.title: IT services for a Kingston print shop
c5.text: A Kingston print shop signed a 24-month contract with a software provider for job-tracking services. It accepted the provider's online terms by clicking "I agree". Six months later the provider emailed to say that its price would rise by 12% from next month. During the contract the shop's manager, Mr Winston Clarke, agreed by phone with a technician that a new report would be added at no cost. Later, the provider billed for it. The contract says disputes must go first to negotiation and then to mediation.

questions.q: Hanover Office Furniture's manager phoned the school on 8 June to withdraw the offer. The board then emailed acceptance on 10 June. What is the legal position?
o: A contract exists, because the offer was open until 12 June
A contract exists, because the withdrawal was not in writing
No contract, because the offer was withdrawn before acceptance
No contract, because the board did not reply by telephone
questions.why: An offer can be withdrawn at any time before acceptance if the withdrawal is communicated, even if the supplier said it would stay open, unless the board paid to keep it open. The 10 June email therefore came too late.

questions.q: Suppose the board had emailed its acceptance on 7 June, and the supplier's system received it at once. When would the contract be formed?
o: On 7 June, when the acceptance was received
On 12 June, when the offer would have expired
On the delivery date for the desks
On 8 June, when the supplier read it
questions.why: Where an instant method such as email is used, acceptance is generally complete when the message is received. At that moment the offer had not been withdrawn, so a contract existed.

questions.q: Suppose the board had said nothing by 12 June and then emailed acceptance on 14 June. What is the effect of the 14 June email?
o: It forms a contract, because the board still wants the desks
It forms a contract at the original price on 14 June
It is invalid, and the supplier must reply with a refusal in writing
It is a new offer that the supplier is free to accept or refuse
questions.why: An offer lapses when the stated time ends. A later "acceptance" cannot form a contract; it operates as a fresh offer, which the supplier may accept, refuse or change.

questions.q: If a contract had been formed at J$9,500 a desk with a deposit of 30%, what balance would be due on delivery?
The dealer said the oven "was serviced every year and in perfect order". It had never been serviced. What is this statement?
o: A harmless sales opinion that gives the buyer no legal rights
A false statement of fact that induced the sale: misrepresentation
An invitation to treat that did not form part of any contract
A promise that is void because the dealer gave no consideration
questions.why: A statement of fact that is untrue and persuades a buyer to purchase is a misrepresentation. It was also a term if the parties meant it as part of the agreement. Either way, the buyer has remedies.

questions.q: The "sold as seen; no liability" wording appeared only on the invoice handed over after delivery. How will a court probably treat it?
o: As binding, because Mrs Ricketts kept the invoice afterwards
As binding, because the oven was sold second-hand
As part of the contract, because it appears in writing
As too late to form part of the contract already made
questions.why: An exclusion clause must be brought to the other party's attention and agreed before or when the contract is made. A clause appearing for the first time after the deal is generally not part of it. The dealer also cannot use it to cover a false statement.

questions.q: What should Mrs Ricketts do first?
o: Tell the dealer in writing, keep the evidence, take advice
Keep using the oven until the dealer has replied to her
Hold back her next payments to her other suppliers
Sell the oven to another baker and accept a lower price
questions.why: Prompt written notice and evidence (the engineer's report, emails, invoice) protect her right to set the contract aside. Continued use can be treated as accepting the oven, and delay weakens her case.

questions.q: A dealer sells goods in the course of business. What also helps protect Mrs Ricketts, even without the dealer's statement?
o: The rule that a buyer has 30 days to return anything
The rule that the price of second-hand goods can be refunded in full
Terms implied by the sale of goods law about quality and fitness
A requirement that the dealer provides a service contract
questions.why: The law implies terms into sales by a business, including that the goods match their description and are of satisfactory quality and fit for the purpose made known. Terms of this kind are not removed by wording added after the sale.

questions.q: Mr Hines says he will sign for the supplier, but only directors may sign. What should Mrs Walters do?
o: Accept his signature, because he is an employee of the supplier
Ask him to sign in his own name as well as for the company
Sign now and check his authority when deliveries begin
Ask for written proof of authority, such as a board resolution
questions.why: A company is bound only by people who have authority. Written proof (a resolution or letter of authority) removes the doubt. Relying on an employee's word, or checking after the contract is signed, risks an unenforceable contract.

questions.q: As a public body, what must Mrs Walters follow before choosing the gravel supplier?
o: The supplier's own standard terms, which are usual in the trade
The procurement rules for public bodies, including competition
Her own preference for a supplier she has used before
A spoken understanding reached with a senior officer of the council
questions.why: Public bodies must follow procurement rules designed to ensure fair competition, value for money and accountability. Preference or informal arrangements do not meet those rules.

questions.q: The supplier's friend hints that "a little something" would speed up approval. What is the correct response?
o: Accept only a small amount, and declare it at a later date
Say nothing, but press the supplier for a lower price
Refuse, record the approach and report it under the policy
Accept it, but only after the contract has been signed
questions.why: A payment to influence a public officer is a bribe. Any contract that depends on it is illegal and unenforceable, and the officer may face criminal and disciplinary action. Refuse, record it and report it.

questions.q: The draft lets the supplier stop deliveries at any time with no liability. What should Mrs Walters do?
o: Negotiate it, asking for notice, service levels and remedies
Accept it, because exclusion clauses are always enforced
Strike out the supplier's name and replace it with her own
Sign it, because a court would remove the clause later
questions.why: A one-sided clause that lets one party walk away is a serious risk for a body that needs steady supply. Raise it before signing, and ask for minimum notice and remedies for failure to supply.

questions.q: The dealer failed to deliver. What damages for the replacement unit and delivery are likely to be recoverable?
questions.why: Extra cost of the replacement: J$468,000 − J$420,000 = J$48,000. Add the extra delivery cost of J$9,000 which arose naturally from buying elsewhere: J$57,000.

questions.q: The restaurant also claims J$300,000 for the lost catering job. Why is this unlikely to be recovered?
o: The restaurant did not sign the contract in person
Damages can never include any lost profit at all
The dealer did not know of it, so it was too remote
The catering job was cancelled before 1 December
questions.why: Damages cover only loss that was foreseeable when the contract was made. Special loss that was never communicated to the dealer is generally too remote.

questions.q: Why was it reasonable for the restaurant to buy a replacement unit promptly?
o: Damages cannot be claimed until a replacement has been bought
The duty to mitigate requires reasonable steps to reduce loss
The law requires a buyer to choose the cheapest replacement
A buyer loses all rights if it waits more than five days
questions.why: An injured party must take reasonable steps to limit loss. A prompt, comparable replacement does this, and the extra cost is then claimed as damages.

questions.q: Suppose the dealer had delivered the unit 8 days late and the clause applied. What could the restaurant claim without proving actual loss?
questions.why: Liquidated damages: 8 days × J$12,000 = J$96,000. The sum was fixed in advance as a genuine estimate, so actual loss need not be proved.

questions.q: A different contract said J$500,000 a day for lateness on a J$420,000 unit. How would a court probably treat this?
o: As valid, because both parties signed the contract freely
As a penalty, far above genuine loss, which may be refused
As valid, because the dealer is a business and not a consumer
As a condition that allows the restaurant to rescind
questions.why: A sum far above the genuine loss, intended to frighten a party into performing, is a penalty. Courts may refuse to enforce it, leaving the innocent party to claim its proven loss.

questions.q: The provider says the price will rise 12% from next month. What is the legal position, in general?
o: It cannot change the price alone unless the contract allows it
It may change the price, because it sets the terms of service
The rise is valid if the shop is notified in writing
The whole contract ends, since the provider has breached it
questions.why: A contract can be varied only by agreement, or as the contract itself allows. Check whether the terms let the provider change prices. If they do not, the shop is not bound by the rise unless it agrees.

questions.q: The technician agreed by phone to add a report free of charge, and the provider then billed for it. What should Mr Clarke do now?
o: Ignore the bill and say nothing until the provider chases it
Pay the bill, because spoken agreements never bind anyone
Cancel the contract by telephone with immediate effect
Confirm it in writing and ask for a signed variation
questions.why: A spoken promise by an employee may or may not bind the provider, and it is hard to prove. Confirm it in writing, with date and name, and ask the provider to sign a variation. Good records settle disputes.

questions.q: The contract requires negotiation first and then mediation. What is the best next step if the 12% rise stays in dispute?
o: Go straight to court, since the provider has breached
Hold back all payment until the provider drops the rise
Negotiate in good faith, then mediate if talks fail
Refuse to speak to the provider until it withdraws the notice
questions.why: Parties are expected to follow the dispute process they agreed. Negotiation and mediation are quicker, cheaper and private, and they may preserve a useful business relationship.
